v: Nani’s stylish one-man show with Thaman supplying the real fireworks. An average-to-good thriller that looks slick and sounds terrific, but still leaves you feeling something important is missing.
e: V has the polish expected from Mohana Krishna Indraganti, but never quite finds the extra spark needed to rise above an average-to-good thriller. Nani’s stylish performance and Thaman’s high-octane BGM are the clear highlights, with P. G. Vinda’s cinematography adding plenty of visual flair.
body:
Nani’s one-man show… with Thaman’s terrific BGM doing serious damage alongside him!

Like several Mohana Krishna Indraganti films, V ultimately settled for me in that average-to-good zone where the craft is visible, the performances are solid, yet you still come away feeling that something is missing.

The biggest strength is clearly Nani.

He gets a stylish part and carries it with complete ease, making the darker shade feel enjoyable even when the material around him is not always giving him enough to work with.

Thaman’s high-octane BGM is the other major asset. It injects energy into the film and gives several scenes more punch than they might have had on paper.

Special mention also to P. G. Vinda’s cinematography and a few stylishly mounted action sequences.

Sudheer Babu, Nivetha Thomas and Aditi Rao Hydari all do their jobs well within the limited scope available to them.

There is nothing disastrously wrong with V, but there is also not enough here to make it truly memorable.

For me, it remains a polished average-to-good watch lifted primarily by Nani’s presence, the visuals and that terrific background score.

v: Simple, rooted and beautifully observed. Satyadev is superb, Venkatesh Maha makes the remake feel completely at home in Araku, and a tiny chain of incidents grows into wonderfully satisfying cinema. MUST WATCH.
e: Uma Maheswara Ugra Roopasya proves how powerful a seemingly simple story can become when every department understands its tone. Venkatesh Maha’s direction, the Araku setting, cinematography, dialogues and Satyadev’s wonderfully subtle performance outweigh the film’s slow pace and less memorable songs.
body:
When an extraordinary director like Venkatesh Maha, a sensible producer like Praveena and an actor as talented as Satyadev came together for a Malayalam remake, my first reaction was honestly: why are these people wasting their talent on a remake?

And then I watched Uma Maheswara Ugra Roopasya.

Man… I got my answer 🙏

I had not watched the Malayalam original at that point, but the film immediately reminded me why Malayalam cinema is so admired for finding extraordinary impact inside incredibly simple situations.

The direction, camera work, locations, dialogues, song lyrics, acting and BGM are all top-notch.

The only negatives I can really point to are the songs themselves and the deliberately slow pace.

Satyadev completely nails the role with a subtle yet deeply effective performance.

There is no unnecessary heroism in the way he plays Mahesh. Every small humiliation, hesitation and emotional shift feels believable.

He is also very well supported by practically every artist around him.

What completely blew me away was the chain of ordinary incidents that eventually leads to the film’s major conflict.

Nothing feels artificially designed as a giant cinematic trigger. One small event leads to another, then another, until suddenly this wonderfully human butterfly effect has changed Mahesh’s life.

That simplicity is the beauty of the writing.

And Venkatesh Maha does not merely remake the material — he makes the world feel completely natural in the Telugu and Araku setting.

For me, this is a MUST WATCH.

v: A simple weekend time-pass powered almost entirely by a terrific comic ensemble. Don’t expect much beyond the laughs — but Kunal Kemmu, Vijay Raaz, Gajraj Rao and gang make sure those laughs keep coming.
e: Lootcase does not need a complicated story or technical fireworks to work. Its biggest strength is the cast — Kunal Kemmu, Rasika Dugal, Vijay Raaz, Ranvir Shorey and Gajraj Rao — who turn a straightforward suitcase comedy into an easy, dependable weekend watch.
body:
A good weekend time-pass.

There is honestly not a great deal to analyse about the story or technical departments of Lootcase.

The entire film works mainly because it has assembled such a talented bunch of performers and then simply allows them to have fun with the material.

Kunal Kemmu, Rasika Dugal, Vijay Raaz, Ranvir Shorey and Gajraj Rao ensure that the movie keeps providing steady entertainment.

Special mention to Vijay Raaz and Gajraj Rao, who are especially enjoyable in their villainous avatars 🙏

The humour comes more from the characters and situations than from any huge plot invention, and that is perfectly fine for the kind of movie this wants to be.

If you simply want to kill some time with a decent comedy, go for it.

It will not disappoint you.

Just do not enter expecting anything much beyond that easy entertainment.

v: A dark murder mystery that proves bold content does not need cheap shock value. Vintage-RGV-style lighting, Nawaz and Radhika at their best, and a satisfying final twist make the slow pace easy to forgive.
e: Raat Akeli Hai handles murder, abuse and family secrets with far more restraint than its dark premise might suggest. Honey Trehan avoids unnecessary nudity or shock tactics, while the lighting, camera work, Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Radhika Apte create a beautifully moody mystery whose only real drawback is its pace.
body:
Raat Akeli Hai is a very well-made murder mystery with a dark underlying subject.

With a title like this, a Netflix release and a story touching on sexual abuse, it would be easy to assume the film will automatically take the no-holds-barred route — cuss words everywhere, nudity, sex and over-the-top violence simply because the platform allows it.

What I liked is that the movie does almost the complete opposite.

The director seems determined to prove that bold content can still be handled cleanly and with restraint.

The subject remains uncomfortable where it needs to be, but the film does not depend on cheap shock value.

The lighting and camera angles throughout the movie repeatedly reminded me of vintage RGV, and I was completely bowled over by that visual mood.

And when you have actors like Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Radhika Apte, you naturally expect strong performances.

They do not disappoint.

The only real negative I can point to is that the film is a little slow.

But that becomes easy to overlook when the performances, atmosphere and final twist are working this well.

For anyone who likes bold content handled with a clean, controlled approach, this is a MUST WATCH.
